newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Shanghai Industrial seen beating profit forecast.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai Industrial seen beating profit forecast.

text.p: Shanghai Industrial Holdings Ltd, the red-hot investment arm of the Shanghai municipal government, is expected to beat its own 1996 net profit forecast when it releases results on Thursday, analysts said on Tuesday.
The popular, diversified China play listed on the Hong Kong stock market is expected to post net profit of HK$340 million to HK$364 million (US$44-47 million) for calendar 1996.
The company forecast net profit of not less than HK$310 million in its initial public offering prospectus last year.
The extra profit was expected to come from acquisitions and additional interest income, analysts said.

Shanghai Industrial's tobacco business is set to be the main contributor to 1996 profit, accounting for about 70 percent of total earnings, said Xue Lan, an investment analyst at SocGen-Crosby Securities.
She said this would be followed by the printing business, which should contribute about 11 percent.
"The excess profit (above the company's forecast) is from the interest income generated by the oversubscription money at their initial public offering," said Elvic Ng, an analyst at Vickers Ballas.
Shanghai Industrial listed its shares in May 1996. Its initial public offering was 157 times oversubscribed.
Analysts said additional income would come from the six projects acquired in November last year including infrastructure, automotive, food and commercial projects.
Shanghai Industrial's long-term strategy is to diversify its operations through investing in other businesses and projects, mainly in Shanghai.
This concept has driven the stock more than 350 percent higher than its IPO price of HK$7.28 per share. The stock closed the morning session on Tuesday up HK$0.10 at HK$33.30.

"What people are looking at is the asset injection concept, and this is a very solid concept since we see it as a vehicle for the Shanghai municipal government to privatise its infrastructure and industrial projects," Ng said.

The stock is trading at more than 30 times 1997 earnings and would be extremely expensive if it were not backed up by the prospects of being able to buy good quality assets at attractive prices from its parent, analysts said.

They said Shanghai Industrial was considering buying more projects from its parent later this year and some put the size of the next possible purchase at HK$5.0 billion, saying infrastructure projects were large and expensive.
But Xue said any purchases probably would be smaller than its HK$2.7 billion November acquisition.
"I personally believe the company needs a consolidation before it goes for another major acquisition," she said.
Analysts estimated full year net profit of between HK$700 million and HK$730 million.
